Paper:
title: Foundations for Investigations of Agentic AI Systems from the Forensic Analysis of OpenClaw
summary: Agentic AI systems are increasingly deployed as personal assistants and virtual employees, and are likely to become a common object of digital investigations and incident response. Yet little is known about how their internal state and actions can be reconstructed during forensic analysis, and systematic forensic approaches remain largely unexplored. We present the first empirical forensic study of a personal AI assistant, with OpenClaw as a case study. We examine its technical design via static code analysis and apply differential forensic analysis to identify recoverable traces across stages of the agent interaction loop. We classify and correlate these traces, structuring the examination around representative investigative questions. We propose a five-plane agent artifact taxonomy that captures recurring investigative patterns; its structural completeness is assessed by cross-mapping against published artifact inventories of two related AI systems. To aid investigations, we release an open-source artifact-extraction tool with a machine-readable schema. Finally, we highlight a foundational challenge: LLM-mediated execution adds both an abstraction layer and substantial nondeterminism to trace generation. Because tool selection and state transitions are co-determined by the model, the execution environment, and the evolving context, identical inputs need not yield identical traces.

Paper:
title: Fault-Tolerant Offloading Framework for Real-Time Applications in Mobile Edge Computing
summary: This paper studies a Deadline-constrained task Offloading and resource Allocation Problem (DOAP) in a backhaul-network-enabled Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) system with both bandwidth and computational resource constraints. The goal is to maximize the total inference accuracy improvement across all tasks. We formulate this problem, denoted as $\mathbf{P}$, as an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) problem and show it is NP-hard via a reduction from the maximum-weight three-dimensional matching problem. To address $\mathbf{P}$, we develop $\mathtt{FastSA}$, a linear-time $\frac{1}{10}$-approximation algorithm based on the local-ratio technique. To the best of our knowledge, $\mathtt{FastSA}$ provides the first constant-factor performance guarantee for backhaul-network-enabled DOAPs. In addition, we introduce a fault detection and recovery framework that enables robust MEC operation under backhaul link and edge server failures. Experiments using profiled image classification workloads and real-world taxi traces show that $\mathtt{FastSA}$ achieves an average accuracy improvement of $25.6\%$ over benchmark algorithms under fault-free conditions while maintaining the lowest runtime. Under fault-injected scenarios, our framework reduces performance degradation by an average of $12.8\%$, demonstrating its effectiveness in fault handling.

Paper:
title: Do We Need Asynchronous SGD? On the Near-Optimality of Synchronous Methods
summary: Modern distributed optimization methods mostly rely on traditional synchronous approaches, despite substantial recent progress in asynchronous optimization. We revisit Synchronous SGD and its robust variant, called $m$-Synchronous SGD, which can be interpreted as a method with a backup-worker strategy, and theoretically show that they are nearly optimal in many heterogeneous computation and communication scenarios, which is somewhat unexpected. We analyze the synchronous methods under random times and adversarial partial participation of workers, and prove that their time complexities are optimal in many practical regimes, up to logarithmic factors. While synchronous methods are not universal solutions and there exist tasks where asynchronous methods may be necessary, we show theoretically that they are sufficient for many modern heterogeneous computation and communication scenarios.

Paper:
title: Bitcoin-IPC: Scaling Bitcoin with a Network of Proof-of-Stake Subnets
summary: Despite holding over $1.7T in value, Bitcoin scales poorly: Layer-1 (L1) processes only a few transactions per second, and Layer-2 (L2) solutions suffer from operational and liquidity fragmentation that requires external bridges for cross-chain connectivity.
  We present Bitcoin-IPC, a protocol that horizontally scales Bitcoin via permissionless, interconnected, programmable Proof-of-Stake L2 subnets staked in L1 BTC. Subnets leverage Bitcoin L1 for interconnectivity, settlement, and security, including Sybil protection, equivocating validator slashing, unilateral exit for honest stake, long-range attack protection, and compromised subnet firewalling. Bitcoin-IPC cross-subnet transfers involve only source/destination subnet validators and L1, with no external bridges or per-path liquidity lock-up. Embedded and batched in Bitcoin's witness mechanism, cross-subnet settlements can approach 6 vB per transfer, 23x less than a native L1 payment. Filling Bitcoin blocks with such batches corresponds to L1 monetary throughput of about 273 transfers per second, without modifying Bitcoin.

Paper:
title: CHERI-D: Secure and efficient inline object ID for CHERI temporal memory safety
summary: We propose CHERI-D, an architectural extension to CHERI that supports efficient temporal memory safety. Efficient memory safety is an increasing priority for programming languages, operating systems, and hardware designs, and CHERI is a leading hardware/software system that provides native spatial safety and a foundation for temporal memory safety. Due to CHERI lacking intrinsic architectural support for temporal memory safety, the state-of-the-art CHERI temporal safety solution, Cornucopia Reloaded, is a software-based solution that provides use-after-reallocation (UAR) protections instead of the stronger use-after-free (UAF) mitigation, and suffers performance overhead due to delayed reallocation and revocation. CHERI-D associates object identification (ID) metadata with capability pointers to provide temporal integrity of allocations. CHERI spatial safety allows CHERI-D to store object IDs safely inline with allocation data, potentially within unused fragmentation. Evaluated in simulation and in hardware, CHERI-D significantly reduces the revocation overhead of Cornucopia Reloaded while allowing it to support strict use-after-free mitigation.

Paper:
title: LeakBench: Auditing Reward Hacking through Prediction-Time Leakage in Clinical Modeling Agents
summary: Autonomous clinical-modeling agents can optimize predictive performance while violating conditions that make a model usable. We introduce LeakBench, an executable, guideline-derived audit suite that tests agent decisions for prediction-time leakage, calibration, site-level evaluation, support awareness, and decision-curve net benefit. LeakBench combines a synthetic task with known failure structure and two real-data settings: MIMIC-IV (430k admissions) and governed multi-hospital inpatient record front-page (MHFP) data. Our primary analysis uses reward hacking descriptively, without attributing intent: an agent selects prediction-time-invalid inputs because they improve its validation reward. A deterministic optimizer and every evaluated unconstrained local-model configuration select a fatal leaking feature. In fully logged September 2026 A/B runs, DeepSeek Flash and GPT-6-astra each leak in 10/10 unconstrained runs and 0/10 runs with an explicit admission-time constraint. This contrast is version-sensitive: a blinded Claude/Fable-5.1 chat run does not leak in either condition, while explicit-constraint violations appear only in a historical August 2026 slice lacking raw trajectories. Replacing AUROC with AUPRC does not remove leakage selection. Renaming or disguising the leaking inputs changes neither selection nor provenance-based detection; a name-based filter fails. A deterministic provenance verifier-in-loop removes the leak, making the LLM repair loop defense-in-depth. Specific verifier feedback clears fatal leakage in a hosted agent, and a three-seed ablation finds principle-only feedback clears decision-level defects, though these mitigation results are limited. LeakBench treats trustworthy clinical prediction as a property of an agent's modeling process, not merely its score; it is an audit testbed with known-failure controls, not yet an expert-validated benchmark.

title: Blame-aware Recomposition for Secure Compilation Proofs of Low-Level Compartment Isolation
summary: The security guarantees of existing formally verified compilers for compartmentalized programs in unsafe languages like C stop at a rather high level, assuming a built-in protection mechanism and a block-based memory model. Verifying a concrete, low-level enforcement mechanism for compartment isolation is still a major challenge for current proof techniques. Paper:
title: From GAN-Based Models to GPT-5: A Taxonomy-Guided Study of Human Performance in Detecting Deepfake Face Images
summary: Generative models for deepfakes have rapidly evolved from GAN-based architectures to diffusion models and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, empirical research on human performance in detecting deepfake face images has not kept pace. It remains unclear if (and how) detection performance varies across generative models and whether model-specific training improves detection more effectively than general-purpose training. In this paper, we propose the \emph{Deepfake Face Artifact Taxonomy} (DFAT), a cross-model taxonomy of human-recognizable visual artifacts in deepfake face images, based on which we build both general-purpose and model-specific training materials. Through an online experiment ($n = 524$), we examined human performance in detecting deepfake face images and evaluated training efficacy across five representative generative models: three GAN-based, one diffusion-based, and one MLLM (GPT-5). Our results show that participants' detection accuracy was strongly model-dependent and that images generated by more recent and advanced models were not necessarily harder to detect. After training, participants achieved significant performance gains across most conditions, and their improvement varied by model. Notably, model-specific training generally yielded greater numerical gains than general-purpose training. In a five-month follow-up test ($n = 342$), we observed no significant decline in detection accuracy and no significant increase in perceived stress. Overall, our findings provide actionable insights for designing effective, sustainable, and targeted training programs to counter the growing threat posed by deepfakes.

Paper:
title: Task-aware Kernel Stein certificates for Rényi differential privacy
summary: Rènyi differential privacy, based on Rènyi divergence, has become a notion of choice for privacy guarantees. However, outside the Gaussian setting, Rènyi divergence can be difficult to compute. In particular, Rènyi differential privacy guarantees that exploit task-specific information, as in Rènyi Pufferfish privacy, can be challenging. Paper:
title: SpanGuard: Decoupling Instruction Localization from Authorization for Lightweight IPI Defense
summary: LLM-based guardrails are effective against indirect prompt injection (IPI), but their performance depends heavily on model capability: as the guardrail model becomes smaller or weaker, detection degrades substantially. This raises a natural question: can we retain strong IPI defense while relying only on a small LLM? To understand why, we revisit what an LLM guardrail actually does. Detecting IPI requires simultaneously locating potentially injected instructions within heterogeneous tool outputs and judging whether they are authorized by the user's request. We find that the difficulty for small models arises largely from satisfying both requirements jointly, rather than from either subproblem alone. This suggests a different path to lightweight defense: explicitly decoupling localization from decision-making. In particular, localization needs no strong language-model reasoning, since injected instructions are often semantically discontinuous with their surrounding content and can be partitioned into local regions via lightweight unsupervised segmentation. Once the observation is partitioned this way, the remaining authorization check becomes a localized judgment that a small LLM can handle. Building on this insight, we design a lightweight IPI guardrail that performs attack-agnostic localization followed by block-level authorization judgment with a small language model. By separating where to look from what to decide, our approach substantially reduces the capability required of the guardrail model while preserving strong defense performance. Empirically, our guardrail achieves a 0.32% attack success rate with negligible loss in benign utility while remaining effective with substantially smaller models. These results show that strong IPI defense need not rely on strong LLMs when localization and decision-making are explicitly decoupled.

Paper:
title: Flipping Minds by Flipping Bits: Decision-Level Cognitive Hijacking of Large Language Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been widely applied in high-stakes decision-making scenarios such as corporate strategy, and users are increasingly relying on their outputs. However, the deep integration of open-source model sharing ecosystems with LLM-powered critical decision-making applications also introduces critical risks: if an attacker can manipulate the model's cognitive stance, they can indirectly influence the judgments and actions of downstream decision-makers. This paper defines such threats as decision-level hijacking. Existing attacks fail to achieve targeted cognitive manipulation without triggering prohibited content or degrading model functionality. To fill this gap, this paper reveals that Bit-Flip Attacks (BFAs) can serve as an attack vector for inducing decision-level hijacking, requiring no real-time interaction or control over the training process, and only a minimal number of weight bits need to be flipped after deployment to achieve stealthy, low-cost, and persistent cognitive manipulation. Therefore, we propose CogBias, a cognitive bias injection framework for LLMs. CogBias converts subjective preferences into optimization signals via a differentiable sentiment evaluator, uses a multi-objective loss to jointly constrain multiple dimensions, and constructs BitScout to locate critical bits, achieving targeted cognitive intervention under an ultra-sparse flip budget. Experiments on Llama-3.2-3B, Mistral-7B, and Qwen2.5-14B, as well as on the commercial recommendation and controversial factual topic scenarios, demonstrate that flipping only a small number of bits stably induces significant stance shifts on target topics, while the impact on non-target tasks and overall output distribution is limited. This work demonstrates that minute perturbations to low-level weight data suffice to undermine the high-level value alignment of LLMs.

Paper:
title: SPLASH: Contrastive Audit Pressure for Detecting and Localizing Security Hallucinations in Generated Code
summary: Code generated by large language models often passes every functional test while remaining insecure. These security hallucinations are common, written with high confidence, and repeated across samples, so neither the generator's own uncertainty nor static analyzers reliably catch them. We introduce SPLASH, which is guided by a new measure called audit pressure. It contrasts teacher-forced log-probabilities for the generated program under a security review and a style review. Aggregated to statements and programs, and grounded in a probabilistic model of competing edits, audit pressure allows SPLASH to choose the secure program among a model's candidate programs and locate the vulnerable statement, with no model training, CWE-specific rules, or internal access to the generating model. Paper:
title: PTOPOFL: Topology-Guided Personalised Federated Learning with Persistent-Homology Client Descriptors
summary: Clustered and personalised federated learning (FL) needs a signal telling the server which clients should share a model. Most methods derive it from losses or model updates that must be recomputed during training. We study pTopoFL, which derives it once, before training, from a compact persistent-homology (PH) descriptor of each client's feature distribution: the server clusters clients on these descriptors, weights them within clusters, and runs blended clustered local gradient descent, returning one personalised model per cluster. For strongly convex, smooth losses we analyse the complete procedure: for any partition, one round is a contraction with factor (1-eta*mu)^tau; the fixed point is characterised by a local-step drift bound, an exact formula for the effective strength of blending (which yields a calibration rule) and a stochastic floor exposing a bias-variance trade-off of clustering; and personalisation lowers the heterogeneity floor in proportion to a measurable share of the dispersion of client optima. Experiments on synthetic federations, a label-skew benchmark and a real four-hospital dataset confirm the theory and delimit the method. When feature geometry and decision rules co-vary, the PH partition recovers the latent client groups, including differences a linear-subspace descriptor misses, and pTopoFL is competitive with the strongest clustered baselines; on the real federation it lowers the test log-loss of FedAvg from 0.463 to 0.438, on par with the best personalised methods. When heterogeneity is invisible in feature geometry, it offers no advantage over FedAvg. pTopoFL transmits model parameters and is no more private than FedAvg; we give a record-level differential-privacy accounting and show that privatising the descriptor destroys the partition. Code reproduces every number.

Paper:
title: NIOCIS: Typed-Decision Next-Hop Routing with Node-Conditioned Option Spaces for Tool-Use Agents
summary: Tool-use agents pay per decision: at each hop a language model re-reads the state and thinks for seconds, though its actions are finite and decisions recur. We present NIOCIS, a routing layer that folds execution logs into a loop-collapsed action graph (forward transitions plus recovery back-edges) answering one typed question: which declared option at a state, plus stop, does the fleet take next? A small model reads a calibrated distribution over them in one pass, emitting no text. On 1,615 production security-operations episodes we measure what the layer replaces, returns and is bounded by. Replaces: the typed encoder matches the logged next hop on 32.2% of the 3,875 held-out decisions (34.9% within the declared options) in 10 ms of encoder time (19.5 ms for the typed-choice form), against 2.2 s per LLM hop; two feature readouts reach 32.8% and 32.3%, an ordering the paired test does not resolve, so the typed layer is chosen for cost, not a separated lead. Tuning: jpt-4b reaches 9.9% zero-shot and 31.9% fine-tuned, a gap an exact paired test does not resolve (p=0.68), at 244 ms. Returns little: the realised hop falls outside the declared options for 7.9% of decisions and outside the model's top twenty for 9.3%; the most confident 15% holds 91.9% accuracy. Bounded: a cross-trace leave-one-out test puts the released state's ceiling at 25.6--44.9% as the state key grows more specific, i.e. repeated states disagree more often than they agree; the option-space ablation attributes the gain to per-node candidate restriction (+3.5 points over a flat catalog) rather than graph traversal (zero within its interval); a gated self-evolution loop lifts every arm above its anchor yet ends below full supervision; a confidence-gated cascade loses agreement when the escalation arm is the zero-shot stand-in; and agreement past a third of the fleet needs a state carrying the plan and the observation.

title: Auditor-Assisted Summary-Channel Verification for Hosted LLM Identity Substitution
summary: Hosted LLM services increasingly expose model identity as a product claim, but external users and auditors often cannot inspect which model configuration served a request. We study an auditor-assisted regime in which a trusted auditor enrolls claimed identities and prepares verification material before deployment, while audit-time verification uses only the claimed identity and released output, without runtime access to model internals, inference logs, routing decisions, or provider metadata. We propose SUMMARK, a summary-channel watermarking framework that uses user-visible reasoning summaries as a keyed audit surface. During setup, SUMMARK constructs identity-specific vocabulary carriers, trains lightweight summary adapters, and calibrates per-identity thresholds. At deployment time, a keyed statistical test assesses whether the released summary is consistent with the claimed identity and, when needed, attributes the most likely enrolled identity. Across model families, scales, and task domains, SUMMARK reliably detects cross-family and cross-scale substitutions at low false-positive rates while preserving task-facing answer quality. We further study FP16->INT8/INT4 precision-consistency diagnostics and robustness under bounded post-processing, rewriting stress tests, and text-only spoofing, revealing both strong performance and clear failure boundaries. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/trinitr0toluene/Summark.

Paper:
title: Revisiting Cauchy-Schwarz Norm Bounds for SDC Detection in LLM Inference
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) execute billions of floating-point operations per output token across many hardware accelerators. At this scale, hardware-induced faults can bypass system-level detection mechanisms and cause Silent Data Corruption (SDC). Algorithm-Based Fault Tolerance (ABFT) is the state-of-the-art technique for protecting matrix multiplication from such faults, but it incurs non-negligible computational overhead and requires thresholds to distinguish hardware-induced errors from floating-point roundoff. In this paper, we revisit Cauchy--Schwarz Norm Bounds (CSNB) as a low-overhead alternative for detecting SDC during LLM inference. We compare CSNB against ABFT through controlled fault injection and evaluate the runtime overhead of both verification and threshold determination across multiple model sizes, batch sizes, and generation lengths.

title: RAGLeak: Supply-Chain Privacy Backdoors in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enables large language models to access external knowledge during inference, but its reliance on external knowledge bases also introduces new attack surfaces. Paper:
title: CyberArena: Benchmarking AI Agents in Live Symmetric Attack-and-Defense Combat
summary: AI agents are demonstrating increasingly strong offensive and defensive cybersecurity capabilities in the real world. Current benchmarks mostly evaluate agents in isolation against static targets. Real cyber operations, however, are dynamic and coupled: security postures constantly change as attackers and defenders adapt to each other in real time. Static benchmarks quickly saturate and miss an agent's ability to attack and defend simultaneously under live pressure. To address this gap, we present CyberArena, a dynamic, symmetric adversarial benchmark built around multi-round attack-and-defense combat. In isolated sandboxes, two agents compete under identical rules, acting concurrently as both attackers and defenders over continuously changing services. This converts static targets into evolving, semi-open challenges, directly testing an agent's speed and precision in discovering, exploiting, and patching vulnerabilities. To sustain the benchmark's longevity, an automated agentic pipeline continuously generates, reviews, and validates new environments. Furthermore, because pairwise contests are notoriously hard to quantify, we introduce a dynamical model that maps match dynamics into unified, multidimensional scores across offensive, defensive, and domain-specific capabilities. Evaluating 12 frontier LLM agents across 40 challenges in 466 matches, CyberArena separates model capabilities where single-agent baselines hit a ceiling. The trajectories read like a fight rather than an exam: defenders patch one hole and miss the next and certify repairs on stale evidence, while capable agents think a move ahead, planting backdoors for later rounds and, in one case, writing their own packet sniffer to watch the opponent. Beyond a benchmark, CyberArena serves as an adaptable, scalable experimental platform for future research on cybersecurity agents.

Paper:
title: An Event-Driven System Architecture for a 15-Minute Urban Flood Digital Twin: A Hanoi Case Study
summary: Flash floods in Hanoi submerge roads within minutes of heavy rain onset, yet public flood advisories remain retrospective. Hydrodynamic models could supply forward-looking depth guidance, but they are typically run offline for historical events, and prior studies have not evaluated whether physics-based simulation, spatial serving, and vehicle-aware routing can operate together within a fixed refresh cycle using a cloud solver and a single commodity server. This paper evaluates an end-to-end prototype of an automated flood digital twin designed to meet a 15-minute refresh cycle under data scarcity. The architecture organizes execution into decoupled, event-driven workflows that chain weather-gated 3Di simulations through hydraulic restart states, serve flood depths through a dual-track spatial layer, and publish road-edge depths via standardized output contracts. Evaluated on a 57-run storm replay in the My Dinh and Tay Mo sector of Hanoi driven by satellite rainfall estimates, every cycle completed within the 15-minute deadline, publishing a ready edge table at a median of 537 s after slot start. Indexed raster tiles resolved point-depth lookups in a median of 0.54 ms (277 times faster than un-tiled rasters), while pre-rendered vector tiles served web maps without database queries. These findings demonstrate that a commodity server coupled to a cloud solver can sustain the 15-minute operational cycle and decouple routing policies from simulation internals. Because simulated depths were not validated against field gauges and the replay used observed satellite rainfall, the results establish system feasibility rather than forecast accuracy or route safety.

Paper:
title: Secure Agentic Coding through Counterexample-Grounded Feedback
summary: As coding models and agent harnesses become more capable, reliable security verification is becoming a central bottleneck. Improving secure code generation requires a signal whose reported progress remains aligned with actual program behavior under optimization; otherwise, an optimizer can improve the signal's verdict without removing the underlying vulnerability. Existing model-based approaches require models to either infer program behavior from source code or specify correct outcomes for adversarial tests, placing substantial reasoning demands on the security signal. We introduce \falcon{}, a counterexample-grounded verification framework that separates attack exploration from behavioral verification and connects them through execution traces of the program under test. In test-time repair, \falcon{} yields substantially stronger held-out functional-security gains than alternative security signals across secure code generation benchmarks, while preserving or improving functionality. As an RL reward, \falcon{} also outperforms static-analysis and learned rewards on held-out functional-security, even when all policies successfully optimize their respective training rewards. Combining \falcon{} with either proxy reward further improves held-out performance, suggesting that execution-grounded feedback can mitigate reward overoptimization while preserving useful guidance from existing security signals.

Paper:
title: Budgeted Attack Scheduling for LLM Red-Teaming: The Roles of Static Priors, Semantic Guidance, and Online Feedback
summary: As jailbreak attacks against large language models (LLMs) become increasingly diverse, red-teaming has come to rely on large libraries of jailbreak prompts and attack strategies to evaluate the robustness of victim models and their defense settings. However, attack effectiveness is highly condition-dependent: an attack that succeeds under one victim-defense setting may fail under another, while exhaustively evaluating the full attack library for each setting incurs substantial token and monetary costs. This motivates studying how jailbreak attacks should be prioritized under a limited attempt budget for efficient robustness evaluation. In this work, we formalize this problem as budgeted attack scheduling over a fixed attack library and investigate three complementary signals under a fixed victim-defense condition: (1) static historical attack success rate (ASR) priors; (2) semantic guidance from LLMs; and (3) online feedback from earlier queries. Building on these signals, we design four scheduling strategies and evaluate them across three victim models and three defense settings on GPT-5.2. Extensive experiments clearly characterize the conditions under which each signal is most effective. Historical ASR provides a strong initialization, but its reliability degrades under defense-induced distribution shifts. Semantic guidance consistently improves or matches static prior-based scheduling in the cold-start regime, while online feedback becomes particularly valuable when transferred priors become stale. Semantic guidance and online feedback can also partially compensate for missing historical priors. Taken together, these findings characterize budgeted red-teaming as an attack scheduling problem in which historical priors, semantic guidance, and online feedback play complementary roles.

Paper:
title: SMS-delivered network-initiated SUPL on Pixel 8: a privacy assessment
summary: A SUPL\_INIT message is a network-initiated trigger that can be sent to a handset using an SMS to unilaterally start a location session: on receipt, the handset is instructed to determine its own position and report it, together with an identifier such as its IMSI, to a server specified in the message, without any action by the phone's user. We find no privacy issue: the handset never sends location data to an attacker-chosen server as a result of an unsolicited SUPL\_INIT delivered by SMS. We also examined an iPhone 8 (Qualcomm modem, iOS 16.7.11). On the handset studied SUPL is disabled, so it ignores any SUPL\_INIT and opens no SUPL connections of its own. More generally, iOS acts on a SUPL\_INIT only during an emergency call, and connects only to a server matching the carrier's configured one.

Paper:
title: AURA-Eval: Evaluation Framework for Acting Under Risk Awareness in LLM Agent Trajectories
summary: LLM agents are increasingly taking actions with real consequences, yet safety evaluations often reduce their behavior to a final safe/unsafe outcome, obscuring whether the agent recognized the risk and how it responded. We introduce AURA-Eval, a framework for evaluating whether agents recognize contextual risk and adapt their behavior accordingly. AURA-Eval truncates tool-use trajectories at safety-critical decision points and asks the evaluated model to generate the next thought and action. It creates controlled scenario variations along six risk mechanisms: harm intensity, scale, target susceptibility, system dependency, oversight, and reversibility. It also creates paired scenarios that preserve the underlying goal but differ in whether safe fulfillment is available, allowing unsafe compliance and over-refusal to be evaluated together. An LLM-judge panel, validated against human annotations, evaluates each continuation along three axes: risk detection from the reasoning trace, and action type and safety from the action. From 157 R-Judge seed trajectories, we construct 1,249 evaluation items and evaluate 20 frontier, open-weight, and safety-tuned models. Across all 20 models, unsafe-action rates are higher when no safe path for request fulfillment is available than when one is; for frontier models, the rates are 27-40% versus 5-7%. When a safe path exists, frontier models rarely refuse; when none exists, they most often propose an alternative. Open-weight models, by contrast, more often execute the request than propose alternatives and act unsafely on 58-83% of items. Controlled risk-mechanism analyses further show particularly high unsafe rates under changes to oversight and scale; removing pre-execution oversight flips 52.3% of cases that were safe on the corresponding original scenario to unsafe.

title: PQC Migration of IPsec: Reliable Composite Key Sharing Mechanisms in IKEv2
summary: The threat of quantum computers breaking classical cryptographic is accelerating the adoption of quantum- resistant cryptographic algorithms. Several government agencies have set a tight time-line for upgradation of all system to support post quantum cryptographs. We study post-quantum migration of IPSec protocols and their impact on network performance. The large key lengths in Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) cannot fit in a single IP packet leading to IP fragmentation. This can cause failure of security associations and degrade performance of IKEv2 under poor network conditions. Extensive experiments under various network conditions demonstrate that the new approach significantly improves handshake time and energy consumption by avoiding the severe retransmission penalties of the Hybrid handshake mechanism. At 1% packet loss, the handshake time of composite key sharing mechanism is better by atleast 20% than hybrid mechanisms, and the improve- ment get better with higher packet loss reaching 30% at 10% packet loss. Energy consumption follows the same pattern achieving reduction of 29% at 10% packet loss

Paper:
title: Towards Architectural-Level Safety Control: Relocating Hazardous Knowledge into Removable Experts in Mixture-of-Experts Models
summary: Large language models acquire broad knowledge from web-scale corpora during pretraining, including knowledge that could be hazardous if misused. Removing such knowledge from the model itself without degrading general capability is desirable but difficult, as it is deeply entangled with general capability within the same parameters. Existing safety alignment and unlearning methods typically adjust these shared parameters, tending to suppress the expression of hazardous knowledge rather than remove it. As a result, the knowledge remains in the model and is readily recoverable by subsequent fine-tuning. To address this limitation, we propose REX (Relocating into Removable EXperts), a knowledge relocation method that separates hazardous knowledge from general capability at the architectural level. Exploiting the modular structure of Mixture-of-Experts models, REX expands the model with a set of new, physically removable experts designated to hold hazardous knowledge. Through expert expansion, selective gradient masking and routing differentiation, it relocates hazardous knowledge out of the original experts and concentrates it in the new ones. Excising these new experts yields a model suitable for public release. This removal holds consistently across Intern-S2, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B; on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, for instance, excision lowers WMDP-Bio accuracy by 48.4 points while MMLU changes by less than 3 points. Paper:
title: ETH: Data-Balanced Heterogeneous Pipeline Parallelism for Training Large Models
summary: Current heterogeneity-aware training systems for large models balance workloads by assigning unequal numbers of layers across pipeline stages, a strategy aimed at equalizing execution time through a unique pipeline configuration. Paper:
title: When Care Expands and Control Declines: Understanding Digital Privacy in End-of-Life Care
summary: Terminally ill patients generate extensive digital health data through hospital portals, physiological monitoring devices, consumer health applications, and end-of-life care platforms. Yet their ability to control this data is systematically undermined by the structural conditions of terminal care. Patient privacy attitudes span three profiles: fundamental absence of privacy awareness, sustained active management under severe tool constraints, and perception of problems followed by resigned abandonment. Interviews with caregivers and physicians reveal benevolent substitution in the name of care needs, expansion of access beyond the initial task, and unresolved boundaries under absent institutional guidance. Paper:
title: Fundamental Limits of Information-Theoretic Secure Aggregation with User Dropouts in Federated Learning
summary: Secure aggregation enables a server to compute the sum of users' gradients or model updates without revealing individual values. With user dropouts, correlated random keys protect local gradients while allowing recovery of the desired gradient sum. We consider three phases: key distribution, masked-gradient upload, and mask elimination. Users establish correlated keys, upload masked gradients, and provide additional messages to eliminate residual aggregate masks. Existing information-theoretic schemes typically design mask-elimination communication for a prescribed dropout threshold and evaluate its cost under worst-case dropouts across the masked-gradient upload and mask-elimination phases. Such designs cannot adjust communication to actual dropout scenarios. Moreover, the randomness and communication costs of establishing correlated keys remain largely unexplored. To address these limitations, we formulate an adaptive secure aggregation framework under the T-colluding security constraint and construct a single scheme that supports all feasible dropout scenarios by adapting its communication to the actual number of dropouts. We establish converse bounds on four resources: key randomness, key-distribution communication, masked-gradient communication, and mask-elimination communication. The latter two bounds are characterized for each realized dropout set in the masked-gradient upload phase. The proposed scheme achieves the optimal masked-gradient communication rate for every feasible dropout scenario and the optimal mask-elimination communication rate in almost all feasible regimes. Its key rate and key-distribution communication rate are each optimal or within a factor of two of their respective information-theoretic optima. These results characterize the fundamental randomness and communication costs of secure aggregation with user dropouts.

Paper:
title: Mobius Injection: From One-Shot Prompt Injection to Sustained Resource Exhaustion in AI Agent Infrastructure
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have emerged as key intermediaries, orchestrating complex interactions between human users and a wide range of digital services and LLM infrastructures. While prior research has extensively examined the security of LLMs and agents in isolation, the systemic risk of the agent acting as a disruptive "hub" within the user-agent-service chain remains largely overlooked. Mobius Injection composes known indirect prompt injection and persistent agent components through a distinct structural mechanism named Semantic Closure, which induces sustained recursive execution of agent components through a single injection event. We demonstrate that this attack is lightweight for the adversary, can evade traditional volumetric DDoS monitors and input filters calibrated for low false-positive rates, and is highly configurable, allowing for surgical targeting of specific environments or model providers. To evaluate the real-world impact, we conduct extensive experiments across three representative claw-style agents and three mainstream coding agents, integrated with 12 frontier proprietary or open-weight LLMs. Our results demonstrate that Mobius Injection achieves substantial attack success across diverse tasks, driving single-node call amplification up to 51.0x. Under coordinated multi-node pressure, each infected node still drains about 123k--127k tokens on a shared five-GPU backend; benign request latency rises by abou 23x--24x, and coordinated infections eventually saturate shared capacity until benign traffic is effectively denied service.

Paper:
title: FedPix: Learning What to Share with Less Leakage in Federated Intelligence
summary: Existing federated intelligence paradigms primarily focus on how models are trained or aggregated, while overlooking a more fundamental question: \textbf{what information should leave the client?} Existing methods often share model updates that users cannot easily inspect, or data representations that may reveal sensitive information. Moreover, generating these representations can be computationally expensive for resource-constrained clients. We observe that image classification does not require all the visual details needed to reconstruct the original image. This suggests that clients could share less information while preserving task performance. However, learning what to preserve is challenging when the server cannot access raw client data. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{FedPix}, which learns to share compact, visually inspectable images instead of model updates or intermediate features. The key idea is to use the shared representations themselves to learn what information should be preserved and what can be discarded. By balancing task utility and reconstruction resistance, FedPix enables the server to improve the representations without accessing raw client data, while keeping client-side computation lightweight. Extensive experiments on BloodMNIST, CIFAR-10, FashionMNIST, and MNIST demonstrate that FedPix achieves strong reconstruction resistance, with reconstruction PSNR as low as 6.87~dB and synthetic PSNR as low as 6.74~dB. Meanwhile, FedPix reduces client runtime by up to 96.0\% (from 1223~s to 49~s on CIFAR-10), while maintaining competitive classification accuracy of 99.18\% on MNIST, 89.97\% on FashionMNIST, 82.24\% on BloodMNIST, and 65.63\% on CIFAR-10.

Paper:
title: Peer-Relative Trust-Guided Update Screening for Robust Semi-Decentralized Federated Learning under Label-Flipping Attacks
summary: Trust and reputation mechanisms can reduce the influence of malicious clients in federated learning (FL), but strict update filtering is difficult under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data because honest local updates may temporarily reduce performance on a shared validation proxy. Under moderate heterogeneity, the proposed method reaches 98.37% final accuracy while rejecting 95.82% of malicious updates and retaining 90.30% of benign updates; the final benign and malicious trust distributions are completely separated (KS=1.00). Under severe heterogeneity, it reaches 95.25% accuracy, rejects 88.55% of malicious updates, and retains 76.90% of benign updates (KS=0.96). Trust weighting alone preserves slightly higher utility in the most heterogeneous condition, but accepts all malicious submis-sions. The results therefore distinguish influence mitigation from explicit containment and quantify the utility-selectivity trade-off introduced by screening. The study provides an empirically validated off-chain governance core that can feed blockchain-based audit and incentive layers in SDFL.

Paper:
title: How Effectively Do Security Skills Guide Coding Agents in Vulnerability Detection in Linux Kernel?
summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents, such as Claude Code, are increasingly used for security auditing, with task-specific skills providing reusable vulnerability-analysis procedures. However, their effectiveness in detecting real vulnerabilities and the reasons for their failures remain unclear. We conduct the first large-scale empirical study of 37 security skills using Claude Code with four underlying LLMs on 100 real Linux kernel vulnerabilities across ten classes, totaling 14800 runs. We evaluate vulnerability detection at the function, statement, and vulnerability-class levels. Results show that 24.4 percent of runs locate the correct function, 18.3 percent identify both the function and responsible statement, and 15.7 percent correctly classify the vulnerability. Our failure analysis reveals limitations in evidence acquisition, state-relation reasoning, code interpretation, candidate verification, investigation coverage, and reporting. Based on these findings, we propose SKILL-SIF, a self-improving framework that iteratively evolves security skills by learning from missed vulnerabilities and failure patterns. We evolve five top-performing skills using the original benchmark and evaluate them on 100 previously unseen vulnerabilities. SKILL-SIF improves fully correct vulnerability detection by up to eight times (from 2 percent to 16 percent) on unseen vulnerabilities, while aggregate accuracy across four LLMs increases by 1.85 times (from 6.05 percent to 11.20 percent). These findings highlight the limitations of existing security skills and demonstrate the potential of failure-driven skill evolution to improve vulnerability detection in coding agents.

Paper:
title: Cyclic Equalizability Characterized by Parikh Vectors
summary: Cyclic equalizability is a notion introduced by Shinagawa and Nuida in 2025, in the study of card-based cryptography. Informally, a collection of words is cyclically equalizable if, by inserting the same letters at the same positions in all words, they can be transformed into words that are cyclic shifts of one another. Shinagawa and Nuida showed that two binary words of equal length are cyclically equalizable if and only if they have the same Hamming weight. They also posed the problem of characterizing cyclic equalizability over larger alphabets. In this paper, we completely characterize cyclic equalizability for two words over an arbitrary finite alphabet by proving that two words are cyclically equalizable if and only if they have the same Parikh vector.

Paper:
title: AgentLoupe: Kernel-Resident Semantic Causal Labels for AI Agent Observability
summary: AI agents translate user intents into system actions via tool invocations. Accurately attributing these actions to their originating LLM interactions is essential for security auditing, yet existing methods, such as AgentSight, fail for delayed execution and cross-process-lineage behaviors. AgentLoupe employs eBPF to capture TLS plaintext to interpret LLM interactions, and assigns each a kernel-resident semantic label. Paper:
title: Privacy-Preserving Robust Monitoring of Dense-Time Temporal Logic
summary: Motivated by the use of third-party testing, this paper presents a privacy-preserving implementation of the robustness monitoring of Signal Temporal Logic (STL). STL is a specification language for systems whose output traces have real-valued timestamps -- most prominently, cyber-physical systems. Its robust semantics, which assign real rather than binary truth values, are an essential ingredient of systems testing and runtime monitoring. In a number of system testing scenarios, the designer and the tester are separate parties. This testing-as-a-service model is common in software, avionics, and semiconductors, and is growing in importance in the red-teaming of machine learning models. In such a model, the designer seeks to preserve the privacy (or secrecy) of its design, while the tester seeks to preserve the privacy of its collateral, including the detailed specification suite. This paper presents a secure multi-party implementation of the robust semantics using arithmetic circuits. This implementation allows one party, which provides a secret trace, and a second party which provides a secret formula, to jointly compute the robustness without either party being able to learn the other party's secret input. We present a number of algorithmic modifications to the robustness computation to enable an efficient multi-party robustness computation. We also present new, semi-linear, robust semantics for STL that take advantage of the efficiencies of arithmetic circuits. The experimental results demonstrate that not only is this privacy-preserving monitor efficient on its own, but also that it can be used in a testing loop without affecting the speed at which bugs are found during robustness-guided system testing.

Paper:
title: Formalization of Rényi Differential Privacy in Isabelle/HOL (Draft version)
summary: Differential privacy (DP) is a gold-standard definition of privacy designed to evaluate the privacy guarantee of databases. Rényi differential privacy (RDP) is an important variant of DP that gives tight evaluations of machine learning algorithms. These formulations are easy to understand, but evaluating privacy for actual databases is complicated. Even a small change in the database can break its privacy, and evaluations of DP and RDP themselves are complicated. In particular, RDP evaluations in recent studies have become much harder. Therefore, formal verification of them has been studied for over a decade.
  In this paper, we propose an Isabelle/HOL library for formalizing Rényi differential privacy in a general setting. We first formalize RDP for continuous distributions. As a technical basis, we formalize several properties of convex functions and $f$-divergences for nonnegative convex functions. We formalize basic properties of RDP, conversion laws from RDP to DP, the moment accountants in DP, and the Gaussian mechanism and its RDP. Finally, we discuss the stochastic gradient descent mechanism with Gaussian noise and formalize a rough evaluation of its RDP and DP.

Paper:
title: Mask-Aware Execution for Efficient JEPA Training
summary: Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are becoming a core representation-learning primitive and a building block for latent world models across vision, video, audio, brain dynamics, and time series. Despite (potential of) wide deployment, current JEPA training pipelines are inefficient: each input is executed through multiple mask-specific branches, with redundant target-side work, and memory-bound token routing. These costs grow with the number of masks and limit GPU efficiency. We present M-JEPA, a mask-aware execution architecture that restructures JEPA training without changing the learning objective. M-JEPA separates mask-independent computation from mask-dependent routing, enabling shared context encoder execution, fused token routing and slicing with backward support, sparse target encoder execution over the union of target tokens, and masked patch embedding for sparse inputs. The resulting pipeline preserves training semantics while reducing computation, memory traffic, and synchronization overhead. We implement M-JEPA for five JEPA variants and evaluate it on NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Compared against the state-of-the-art baselines, M-JEPA achieves up to 1.7x end-to-end training speedup for 2-10 masks. Separately, with masked patch embedding, 4.75x patch-embedding speedup at high sparsity. These results show that execution restructuring, rather than changes to the JEPA objective, is a key lever for efficient JEPA training.

Paper:
title: SoK: Systematizing LLM Prompt Security: Taxonomies, Datasets, and Unified Evaluation of Attacks and Defenses
summary: Prompt-security claims for large language models (LLMs) are often compared as properties of individual attacks or defenses, although measured harmfulness depends on the target model, access setting, attack and defense configuration, prompt sample, and judger. We systematize 272 studies through three linked, multi-label taxonomies of jailbreak attacks, defenses, and model vulnerabilities. To make these dependencies explicit, we introduce an access-compatible evaluation protocol over configured $\langle M,A,D,S,J\rangle$ tuples and instantiate it in PromptSecurity, an open-source platform that records method settings, outputs, judgments, and query costs. We release two complementary datasets: JailbreakDB, with 445,752 jailbreak system-user prompt pairs and 1,094,122 benign prompts, and PromptSecurity-Eval, with 166,200 harmful-query and 25,800 benign-utility output records. We evaluate 11 target models, 20 attacks, nine defenses, and three automated judgers under a matched, single-turn protocol using 100 harmful queries and separate benign-utility tasks. Lower attack success can reflect failure to execute transformed requests rather than stronger safety; attack-category advantages can reverse when one method is excluded, and attack success varies with assistant choice. Defenses can reduce harmful outputs while degrading benign-task utility or causing backfire. Rejudging identical outputs also shows that measured attack success is sensitive to the behavior supplied to the judger, highlighting the need to report judger configurations alongside ASR. These findings motivate configuration-aware reporting rather than context-free method rankings.

Paper:
title: Cerium: A Multi-GPU Framework for Terabyte-Scale Encrypted Inference
summary: Encrypted AI using fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables inference directly over encrypted queries, providing strong privacy guarantees. However, its computational and memory overheads have limited practical deployment. Custom FHE accelerators improve performance, but rely on advanced manufacturing technologies that limit their accessibility. GPUs offer a more widely available alternative, yet achieving ASIC-class performance on GPUs is challenging. Large models such as LLMs compound these challenges by requiring optimized kernels, terabyte-scale memory management, and efficient execution across multiple devices.
  We present Cerium, a multi-GPU framework for large-scale FHE inference. Cerium combines a domain-specific language, an optimizing compiler, and a runtime system to automatically generate optimized GPU kernels, compress plaintext data, manage terabyte-scale memory footprints, and optimize multi-GPU communication.
  Implemented on NVIDIA GPUs, Cerium outperforms expert-written GPU libraries by up to 2.25x and achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art FHE ASICs, matching the CraterLake ASIC. It is the first GPU system to execute CKKS bootstrapping in under 10 milliseconds, achieving 7.5 milliseconds, and is the first to demonstrate encrypted inference for BERT-Base and Llama3-8B prefill in 8 seconds and 43 seconds, respectively. The Cerium framework is open-source and available at https://github.com/CMU-CAOS/Cerium

Paper:
title: A Trust Ledger and an Execution Check for CPG-Based C-to-Lean 4 Autoformalization: Separating Declined from Silently Incorrect Translations
summary: Verifying large C codebases requires translating them into formally checkable semantics, but most autoformalization work reports a single aggregate success rate that conflates two different failure modes: code the translator declined to handle and code the translator translated incorrectly. We present a deterministic code-property-graph (CPG)-based exporter that translates C source into a small Lean~4 core semantics under a three-tier correctness discipline: hole-free, call-closed, and dynamic-hole-risk, that keeps these modes distinct. Applied to a re-export of the SQLite source tree (8{,}602 functions, over 1.5~million AST nodes), the exporter translates 5{,}222 functions (60.7\%) hole-free, of which only 2{,}134 (24.8\%) are call-closed, a $2.4\times$ gap a single rate would hide. Both figures are reported in a full per-construct trust ledger rather than a single score. Our main contribution is methodological: a protocol for separating constructs that are fundamentally unresolvable by whole-program static analysis (such as public API boundaries) from constructs that only look that way. For example, we retracted our own ``impossible'' classification of function-pointer/vtable dispatch after tracing a concrete counterexample in the target codebase. Separately, a search for ``more holes closed'' surfaced a latent silent-wrong-answer bug: a translation that succeeded with an incorrect result rather than declining, a failure mode we argue is more dangerous than any hole, and one a hole-count-only evaluation would never surface.

title: Large Language Models over Networks: Collaborative Intelligence under Resource Constraints
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming society, powering applications from smartphone assistants to autonomous driving. Yet cloud-based LLM services alone cannot serve a growing class of applications, including those operating under intermittent connectivity, sub-second latency budgets, data-residency constraints, or sustained high-volume inference. Paper:
title: StreamAhead: Real-Time Streaming Video Question Answering via Adaptive Precomputation
summary: Real-time streaming video question answering with vision-language models must answer queries that arrive at any time with low latency while sustaining the video-processing rate required by the application. Existing systems construct key-value (KV) caches for the entire video as it arrives, although a query typically uses only a few of the preceding frames as evidence. This highlights a fundamental trade-off: performing more computation as video arrives reduces query-time computation but can increase processing lag, whereas deferring computation can increase the video-processing rate but requires additional query-time computation for retrieved content.
  We present StreamAhead, an algorithm-system co-design that exploits this trade-off through adaptive precomputation: dynamically controlling how much computation to complete for each video segment before a query arrives. StreamAhead encodes video segments independently and lets each remain at a different representation level, from inexpensive visual features to costly KV caches, completing KV caches only for the retrieved segments when a query arrives. StreamAhead profiles offline the cost of advancing a segment to each representation level. Its runtime uses these profiles to schedule segment computation concurrently with query execution, pipelining it across heterogeneous CPU and GPU resources while maintaining the required video-processing rate. StreamAhead achieves accuracy competitive with state-of-the-art methods with up to 10.4x lower time-to-first-token (TTFT), and up to 5.9x lower TTFT than state-of-the-art streaming systems. It sustains 30 FPS with P95 TTFT under 0.5 s, and up to 57 FPS with P95 TTFT under 2 s. To our knowledge, StreamAhead is the first real-time streaming video QA system with competitive accuracy, setting a new Pareto frontier between video-processing rate and TTFT.

Paper:
title: Fine-Grained Parallel Graph Algorithms Can Be Both Fast and Scalable
summary: Making graph algorithms fast and scalable on traditional architectures and GPUs often involves breaking them into large, coarse-grained computational blocks that access similar regions of memory. We show that graph algorithms, which have tremendous vertex- and edge-level parallelism, can be scaled as fine-grained programs on suitable architectures. Specifically, we investigate graph algorithms on the UpDown architecture and show how this many-threaded, cache-less architecture enables simple, fine-grained parallel graph algorithms to be both fast and scalable. Single-node UpDown performance is 28x (geomean) over an H200 GPU, and that same program scales to 1000's of nodes. We evaluate the system three ways: simulation, analytical projection models, and selected validation studies at scale (simulation of 16,384 UpDown nodes, using 256 supercomputer nodes). These results show the UpDown system can achieve 680K giga-traversed edges per second (GTEPS) for PageRank and 989K GTEPS BFS, exceeding prior results significantly.

Paper:
title: Redefining Hybrid Blockchains: A Balanced Architecture
summary: Blockchain technology has completely revolutionized the field of decentralized finance with the emergence of a variety of cryptocurrencies and digital assets. However, widespread adoption of this technology by governments and enterprises has been limited by concerns regarding the technology's scalability, governance, and economic sustainability. This paper aims to introduce a novel hybrid blockchain architecture that balances scalability, governance, and decentralization while being economically viable for all parties involved. The new semi-centralized model leverages strategies not prevalent in the field, such as resource and node isolation, containerization, separation of networking and compute layers, use of a Kafka pub-sub network instead of a peer-to-peer network, and stakes-based validator selection to possibly mitigate a variety of issues related to scalability, security, governance, and economic sustainability. Simulations conducted on Kubernetes demonstrate the architecture's ability to achieve over 1000 transactions per second, with consistent performance across scaled deployments, even on a lightweight consumer-grade laptop with resource constraints. The findings highlight the system's scalability, security, and economic viability, offering a robust framework for enterprise and government adoption.

Paper:
title: Heuristic-Driven Resource Optimization for Decoupled Memory Channels on FPGAs
summary: Determining OpenCL channel depths for Decoupled Access-Execute (DAE) architectures in High-Level Synthesis (HLS) is critical for balancing performance and hardware efficiency. Conventional static analysis tools often over-provision these memory channels to ensure performance safety, leading to significant resource stranding. This paper presents an expansion of an LLVM-based static analysis framework, originally proposed for automated DAE generation, by introducing a hardware-aware refinement layer. We identify a counter-intuitive Performance Inversion Paradox linked to baseline memory stalls, where high-stall, grid-based kernels reach peak performance at minimal channel depths and suffer up to a 61% throughput degradation when depths are increased. We propose a Heuristic Refinement Layer that optimizes OpenCL channel depths based on this correlation between baseline stalls and performance saturation. Experimental results demonstrate that our expanded framework successfully identifies the Minimal Peak Performance point across various benchmarks. By avoiding the performance traps of standard over-provisioning, we achieve a 2.52x improvement in Resource Efficiency for an illustrative HotSpot application. This approach maintains peak execution speedup while ensuring the leanest possible hardware profile, outperforming conservative tool-based static predictions.

Paper:
title: ATEST: Adaptive Resource-Aware Test-Time Scaling for LLM Inference
summary: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by sampling multiple answers, but fixed sampling budgets ignore both query difficulty and the changing energy cost of inference under GPU contention. We measure up to a 4.1-fold increase in energy for the same four-sample query as GPU load rises. We present ATEST, a resource-aware TTS framework that jointly considers the expected value of additional samples and their current GPU cost. ATEST-Online, its default mode, requires no offline calibration: it incrementally generates samples, estimates the stability of the plurality answer, monitors live GPU conditions, and learns step energy cost online to decide when to stop. ATEST-Calibrated instead selects a per-query budget using offline accuracy and cost models, favoring deployments with stable loads. We evaluate both modes on four reasoning and question-answering datasets using Phi-3-mini on an NVIDIA A100 under controlled varying load, and test transfer to an NVIDIA L40S and Qwen2.5-3B. Across the four A100 datasets, ATEST-Online answers every query without exceeding the energy budget, while achieving the highest or statistically tied accuracy and reducing sampling as load increases. On GSM8K at high load, it achieves 60.0% accuracy with no deferrals, versus 44.0% accuracy and 42.4% deferrals for ATEST-Calibrated. Ablations show that online cost learning drives adaptation to load. Including offline profiling, ATEST-Online uses 42 times less GPU time and 48 times less energy than ATEST-Calibrated for the evaluated workload. Online control trades higher tail latency and lower throughput on short tasks for robustness under varying load; offline calibration remains competitive under stable conditions.

Paper:
title: DECKER: Domain-invariant Embedding for Cross-Keyboard Extraction and Recognition
summary: Acoustic side-channel attacks (ASCA) on keyboards pose a significant security risk, as keystrokes can be inferred from typing acoustics, revealing sensitive information. Prior ASCA studies are limited by small-scale datasets with restricted diversity in users, keyboards, and environments, constraining analysis across devices, microphones, and noise conditions. We introduce HEAR, a dataset designed to study ASCA along three axes: keyboard generalization, noise adaptation, and user bias. HEAR contains recordings from 53 participants using 37 laptop keyboards, collected in three realistic settings: (1) external microphone capture, (2) device microphone capture without network noise, and (3) VoIP-based streaming capture. This enables controlled evaluation across users, keyboards, and environments. On HEAR, we establish an ASCA benchmark spanning conventional features and pre-trained representations from raw audio and spectrograms in unimodal and multimodal settings. We propose DECKER, a domain-invariant keystroke inference framework with four stages: (1) Keyboard Signature Normalization to reduce device coloration, (2) domain-adversarial disentanglement to suppress keyboard identity, (3) supervised cross-keyboard contrastive alignment to enforce key consistency, and (4) Acoustic Style Randomization to synthesize unseen keyboard responses. We further explore sentence-level inference using an LLM-based post-processing layer to refine keystroke sequences via linguistic context. Results on HEAR show DECKER improves keystroke identification over strong baselines, particularly in cross-keyboard and cross-user settings, with further gains from language-model rectification. These findings highlight that ASCA remains effective across diverse users, devices, and noisy environments, underscoring its practical security risk.

Paper:
title: Multi-Criteria Routing for Cryptographic Key Exchange in QKD Networks: Survey, Taxonomy, and a Conceptual Optimization Framework
summary: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) networks enable unconditionally secure key exchange using quantum mechanical principles. However, routing cryptographic keys across multi-hop quantum networks introduces challenges unique to quantum communication. This survey analyzes and classifies 26 routing strategies proposed between 2013 and 2024 for terrestrial, satellite, and hybrid QKD infrastructures. Dynamic, key-aware routing algorithms have been shown to reduce service rejection rates by 25-40% compared to static shortest-path methods by incorporating real-time key pool availability and link error rates. Multi-path strategies improve resilience against trusted-node compromise by distributing keys across disjoint routes, albeit with an increase in key consumption of 30-60%. SDN-based orchestration frameworks emerge as essential enablers of flexible, QoS-aware routing for hybrid networks integrating terrestrial fibers and intermittent satellite links. Critical research directions include reducing dependence on trusted nodes through quantum repeaters or post-quantum cryptography, developing standardized key management interfaces for interoperability, and adopting AI-driven predictive routing for adapting to fluctuating network states. This comprehensive synthesis of routing algorithms, performance trade-offs, and unresolved issues offers practical guidance for engineering secure, adaptable, and large-scale QKD networks capable of meeting real-world deployment demands.

Paper:
title: Efficient Training on Multiple Consumer GPUs with RoundPipe
summary: Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) on consumer-grade GPUs is highly cost-effective, yet constrained by limited GPU memory and slow PCIe interconnects. Pipeline parallelism combined with CPU offloading mitigates these hardware bottlenecks by reducing communication overhead. However, existing PP schedules suffer from an inherent limitation termed the \textit{weight binding} issue. Binding uneven model stages (e.g., the LM head is large) to GPUs limits the pipeline's throughput to that of the GPU with the heaviest load, leading to severe pipeline bubbles.
  In this paper, we propose RoundPipe, a novel pipeline schedule that breaks the weight binding constraint on consumer GPU servers. RoundPipe treats GPUs as a pool of stateless execution workers and dynamically dispatches computation stages across devices in a round-robin manner, achieving a near-zero-bubble pipeline. To ensure training correctness and system efficiency, RoundPipe integrates a priority-aware transfer scheduling engine, a Layerwise Model Consistency Protocol, and an automated layer partitioning algorithm. Evaluations on an 8$\times$ RTX 4090 server demonstrate that RoundPipe achieves 1.48--2.16$\times$ speedups over state-of-the-art baselines when fine-tuning 1.7B to 32B models. Remarkably, RoundPipe enables LoRA fine-tuning of the Qwen3-235B model with 31K sequence length on a single server.
  RoundPipe has been open-sourced as a Python library.

Paper:
title: Adaptive Cyber-Defense for Evolving Attacker Capabilities using Reinforcement Learning and Behavior Trees
summary: Autonomous cyber-defense agents trained using reinforcement learning (RL) are increasingly adopted for defending enterprise computer networks. However, existing approaches may become brittle as attacker capabilities evolve and enable new attack strategies. In this work, we study the problem of adapting defender policies learned in CAGE Challenge Scenario 2 (CC2), a benchmark enterprise network defense scenario, to an extended network scenario with new attacker capabilities represented by new attacker actions. Effective attack strategies that leverage new actions are initially unknown, and therefore attacker policies must be learned before defender adaptation can occur. To address this challenge, we develop adversarial RL (ARL) with behavior trees (ARLBT), which uses reward behavior trees (RBTs) to define progression-based reward functions and condition attacker policies on RBT execution. The proposed RBT incorporates the new attacker actions into structured attack strategies while leveraging parallel execution to generate rewards across multiple network nodes simultaneously. We evaluate ARLBT for learning attacker policies against two baseline defender policies across network scenarios with different sets of new attacker actions and compare against multiple attacker baselines. The results demonstrate that ARLBT improves attacker success compared to ARL using the original CC2 reward function and that conditioning policies on RBT execution can improve sample efficiency. We further show that defender policies can be adapted against the learned attackers, improving robustness to attacks that leverage new attacker actions.

Paper:
title: Spectrum of Liability: Forensically Sound Acquisition of Wireless Evidence for the Reconstruction of Maritime Cyber-Physical Incidents
summary: Modern maritime navigation depends on mandatory wireless inputs, most notably GNSS and AIS, whose reception can be spoofed or jammed. When groundings or collisions occur, liability and safety investigations often turn on whether RF interference corrupted bridge instruments, yet the artifacts typically available (VDR outputs, IBS logs, screenshots, decoded messages) are downstream, lossy, and easy to contest in adversarial proceedings. We introduce a forensically sound acquisition methodology that preserves upstream wireless evidence together with the minimal contemporaneous context needed to interpret it. Our system records coherent, multichannel IQ across relevant bands while simultaneously collecting time-aligned receiver and instrument-state metadata (e.g., decoded AIS/GNSS outputs and NMEA sentences), enabling later re-decoding and physical-layer reanalysis tied to what the onboard stack indicated at the time. To make the record independently auditable, we package samples and metadata into a single append-only forensic envelope that cryptographically binds per-stream hash chains with trusted-time anchors and periodic checkpoints, allowing third parties to detect tampering (modification, truncation, splicing, cross-case substitution) and to verify the claimed recording window. A prototype implementation shows the approach is practical: integrity mechanisms add negligible storage overhead and modest compute cost at operationally relevant multiband capture rates.

Paper:
title: A Common Ancestor of PDL, Conjunctive Queries, and Unary Negation First-order Logic
summary: We introduce and study UCPDL+, a family of expressive logics rooted in Propositional Dynamic Logic (PDL) with converse (CPDL) and universal modality (UCPDL). In terms of expressive power, UCPDL+ strictly contains PDL extended with intersection and converse (a.k.a. ICPDL), as well as Conjunctive Queries (CQ), Conjunctive Regular Path Queries (CRPQ), or some known extensions thereof (Regular Queries and CQPDL). Further, it is equivalent to the extension of the unary-negation fragment of first-order logic (UNFO) with unary transitive closure, denoted by UNTC, which in turn strictly contains a previously studied extension of UNFO with regular expressions known as UNFO$^{reg}$.

We investigate the expressive power, indistinguishability via bisimulations, satisfiability, and model checking for UCPDL+ and CPDL+. We argue that natural subclasses of CPDL+ can be defined in terms of the tree-width of the underlying graphs of the formulas. Paper:
title: SEAL: Towards Persistent Tool Poisoning Attack against LLM Agents via Prefix-Eliciting Trigger
summary: Tool poisoning has emerged as a critical security threat to LLM agents, where adversaries embed malicious instructions in tool descriptions or external resources that enter the agent's context, allowing adversaries to manipulate agent's tool selection process. Extensive experiments across seven representative multi-round scenarios and different models demonstrate the attack effectiveness of SEAL, its transferability across target models, and its resistance to potential defenses.

Paper:
title: Equivalent Non-linear Shift Register Transformations and Espresso
summary: The stream cipher Espresso was designed by E. Dubrova and M. Hell as a hardware-efficient candidate for 5G security. It has two components - a 256-bit binary non-linear feedback shift register (NFSR), with 14 feedback taps, and a 20-variable non-linear output function. However, the security of Espresso with regard to several standard cryptanalytic attacks are estimated using an alternate NFSR, which has only two feedback taps. The above analysis is based on the claim that this alternate NFSR is obtained using a transformation algorithm which preserves the output sequence of the original NFSR. This issue has become all the more significant in the light of recent results on hardware performance evaluations, which assume that the stated equivalence holds.
  This article presents the first successful attempt in settling the above question of Espresso NFSR equivalence. We arrive at our main result by a careful analysis of existing transformation methods relevant to the question. In doing so, we first identify and correct a critical flaw in the proof of a foundational result of E. Dubrova. Next, in the context of Espresso equivalence, we analyze and unify the transformation framework of Dubrova and the one proposed by Yao and Parampalli. Based on our analysis, we have succeeded in transforming the LFSR in an Espresso-equivalent design reported by Yao and Parampalli to the Espresso alternate NFSR. Further, we have obtained a corresponding non-linear output function which achieves output-equivalence with the LFSR design, and hence, with Espresso.

Paper:
title: Estimating the Social Cost of Corporate Data Breaches
summary: While the size of a data breach is typically measured by the number of (consumer, customer, or user) records exposed or compromised, its economic impact is generally measured from the point of view of the corporation suffering the data breach: cost in crisis management, legal fees, drop in stock price, and so on. This study examines whether it is possible to estimate the true cost, or the social cost of a data breach, measured by the impact on its victims and their out of pocket costs. To accomplish this we establish: (1) the estimation of the average direct financial losses of an identity theft (IDT) victim, including the opportunity cost of lost time, and healthcare expenditures associated with distress associated with identity theft; and (2) the estimation of increases in incidents of IDT that can be attributed to a major breach event. Our findings show that the average social cost per victim has declined significantly since 2016. Furthermore, we find that there is indeed a statistically significant increase in the number of IDTs following a mega-breach event when accounting for a discovery lag of 1-2 months post-breach. Applying our model to real-world cases allows us to estimate an upper and lower bound social cost of specific mega-breach events. We find that for the 2009 Heartland and 2013 Target breaches, even the conservative lower bound social cost estimate exceeded settlements by factors of 5 and 16, respectively. In contrast, the 2017 Equifax breach resulted in a lower bound estimate of $263.8 million, falling well within its $700 million settlement cap. While the Equifax upper bound estimate of $1.72 billion in social cost more than doubles this settlement, the narrowing gap between institutional liability and an incident's social cost provides empirical evidence of a market saturation effect that reduces the marginal damage of individual compromised records over time.

title: AdaFedXplain: Adaptive Federated Learning with Explainable AI for Ransomware Detection
summary: Attacks using ransomware have developed into complex multiphase campaigns that target vital infrastructure, resulting in annual damages of billions of dollars.
