Paper:
title: The Window Is in the Reasoning: When LLM Agents Decide to Follow Prompt Injections
summary: LLM agents that read untrusted content can be hijacked by prompt injections. Runtime monitors that try to catch a hijack before the agent acts, and benchmarks that score each task with a single run, share an assumption: whether an agent follows an injection is settled when the injection is read. We test this assumption with branching rollouts that replay an episode exactly up to the step at which the agent reads an injection and then resample the rest of the episode many times, splitting the outcome variance into a part fixed at read time and a part decided afterwards. Across four AgentDojo suites, a Qwen3 agent without thinking is largely decided at read time (0.91 of the outcome variance lies between states); with thinking on, this share drops to 0.62 (95% CI of the drop [-0.38, -0.22]), in the same direction for three attack templates and two success labels. How much is fixed at read time is a property of the model that the same measurement reveals, and thinking lowers the attack success rate of Qwen3 but raises it for two other models. Resampling from reasoning prefixes shows that the decision forms gradually as the agent reasons. Zero-shot chain-of-thought monitors built on cheaper models miss much of what is already decided, whereas stronger monitors, and a lookahead monitor that judges simulated next actions, come close to what the prefix determines. Finally, single-run labels of thinking agents disagree with a rerun up to 35% of the time, so benchmarks need repeated runs per task.

Paper:
title: TUPLE-Bench: Evaluating and Mitigating Privacy-Utility Trade-offs in Typed Decision Models
summary: Typed decision models often return more than a selected category. They also expose probabilities for each candidate and, sometimes, a separate confidence score. These fields support downstream decisions but may reveal information beyond a recipient's authorization. We introduce TUPLE-Bench (Typed decision models' Utility and Privacy Leakage Evaluation Benchmark), a benchmark of paired synthetic cases in which recipients may learn a coarse operational category but not its fine-grained cause. Even when causes are excluded from the candidate set, full outputs enable 62.85%-75.35% recovery on held-out cases, compared with 51.04%-57.64% using only the selected category (50% chance). Full outputs also reduce mean downstream cost in all 27 model-task comparisons. However, confidence fields increase leakage without consistently reducing cost. We further introduce workflow-constrained privacy quantization (WCPQ), which reduces secret recovery while preserving the behavior and cost of specified downstream workflows. Our findings highlight the need to audit decision interfaces field by field and workflow by workflow.

Paper:
title: ABF-Bench: A Verifiable Benchmark for Agentic Blockchain Forensics
summary: Blockchain forensics is adversarial and open-ended: money launderers split, swap, and bridge funds, cut their trail at mixers or custodial services, and change tactics from one incident to the next. Investigators must keep adapting their tracing in response. Yet the immutability of public ledgers preserves every recorded movement in public view, making much of the investigation independently verifiable. We introduce ABF-Bench, an interactive benchmark that makes evidence-backed fund tracing a verifiable agent task, in which every claimed movement must cite ledger records the agent retrieved. A case-to-task pipeline builds well-posed tasks across ledgers: conservative rules halt tracing wherever the records leave a continuation unresolved, and each task's reference graph is the answer those rules determine. Paper:
title: Token-Level Attribution of Multi-Mode LLM Watermarks: Optimal Rule and Belief Weighting
summary: A watermark verifier may hold many modes, i.e., secret keys, and a document may mix spans of different modes with unwatermarked text. Directly reporting the mode with the largest pivotal statistic (pivot) inflates the Type I error, and restoring the nominal level reduces power as candidate modes are added. Paper:
title: Sharing is caring: Attestable and Trusted Workflows out of Distrustful Components
summary: Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) protect private memory and attest initial code and configuration, but neither constrain nor attest shared channels between TEEs or with the untrusted host. Confidentiality thus depends on the functional correctness of all in-TEE code accessing these channels: a single misuse can leak data and compromise a pipeline. This assumption is increasingly untenable for agentic applications that generate code at runtime and cloud pipelines of mutually distrustful components. We present MICA, a confidential-computing firmware extension that decouples confidentiality from trust in in-TEE code. MICA lets tenants define, restrict, and attest channel constraints between TEEs and with the untrusted host, including transitive constraints spanning a pipeline. It extends attestation to groups of communicating TEEs, letting external parties verify the confidentiality properties induced by these constraints across a pipeline. We implement MICA on Arm CCA by extending the Realm Management Monitor with a small policy language, requiring no hardware changes and minor QEMU and KVM changes. Our evaluation demonstrates support for confidential agentic applications and pipeline computations without trusting the functional correctness of in-TEE code. MICA increases the TCB by 7% and incurs infrequent setup costs: 2-4% boot-time overhead, approximately 1.5 s for policy upload, and 246-598 ms for group attestation. Once established, Realm communication is direct, uses protected memory, and requires no MICA intervention or software encryption, yielding up to 14.5 times lower cross-TEE message latency than encrypted communication over untrusted memory.

Paper:
title: The Infinite Mutation Engine? Measuring Polymorphism in LLM-Generated Offensive Code
summary: Malware authors traditionally rely on polymorphic techniques to produce variants within a malware family, complicating detection. Generative AI enables attackers to automatically synthesize structurally diverse payloads with identical behavior, raising the question of how much evasion Large Language Models (LLMs) actually provide. Recent work has assumed that LLMs can produce highly polymorphic payloads, leaving unquantified the variation that emerges when an attacker repeatedly generates a payload, or explicitly instructs the model to avoid prior implementations. In this work, we address this gap by measuring the polymorphic capacity of a commercial model (Claude Opus~4.6) acting as an automated malware generator. We build a dual-agent, four-stage pipeline that generates, tests, and refines a data-exfiltration payload comprising file traversal, encryption, exfiltration, and integration. We produce payloads under two settings: (a) functional prompting, and (b) explicit prompting injecting a structured history of prior variants. Evaluating structural (TEDs) and semantic (embeddings) variance, we find that explicit prompting fragments the structural space, creating variants that are hard to cluster for some ML classifiers. This structural diversity is operationally cheap, costing \$0.41--\$0.73 per validated payload. However, static n-gram analysis reveals that because the LLM treats inter-module boundaries as immutable, a single static signature targeting them achieves 100\% detection across all generations. Finally, a complementary evaluation of seven local small language models (SLMs) (20M--1.5B parameters) confirms that current open-weights architectures lack the generative stability required for reliable polymorphic synthesis.

Paper:
title: Uniform-Price Mechanism Design for Automated Market Makers
summary: Automated market makers (AMMs) are central to decentralized exchanges, but their reserve curves make mechanism design different from classical double auctions. We study a batch double auction with buyers, sellers, and a liquidity-nondecreasing AMM: post-trade reserves must have weakly larger product than the initial reserves. Each user has two-dimensional private information: a unit value and a demand or supply quantity. User trades clear at one uniform price subject to AMM feasibility. The objective is user-side trading volume, benchmarked against the optimal feasible individually rational (IR) uniform-price allocation. We give a randomized uniform-price mechanism based on binary quantity buckets. It randomly chooses one of three clearing modes: peer-to-peer matching, AMM sales to buyers, and seller sales to the AMM. Every deterministic realization of the mechanism is ex-post feasible and satisfies IR and weak quantity incentive compatibility: conditional on any quantity report, truthful unit-value reporting is dominant whenever it gives a non-negative utility, no unit-value deviation gives a positive utility if the truthful one doesn't, and users cannot benefit by under-reporting the quantity together with their truthful unit value. Let $V^\ast$ be the optimal feasible IR uniform-price volume without incentive constraints, and let $γ=\bar q/\underline q$, where $\bar q$ and $\underline q$ are the quantity-domain bounds. For $γ\ge1$, the mechanism achieves an expected trading volume of $ Ω(1/(1+\logγ)^2)V^\ast - O(\bar q). $ We also show that full incentive compatibility over the two-dimensional type space forces a worst-case approximation ratio of $O(1/γ)$ at every prescribed initial reserve ratio, even when both AMM reserves are scaled by an arbitrarily large common factor and the optimal volume $V^\ast$ is arbitrarily large relative to $\bar q$.

title: From Billion-Scale to Million-Scale Language Models: Operational Capabilities for Embedded Post-Exploitation
summary: Small Language Models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for resource-constrained environments due to their low computational footprint. These characteristics also make them candidates for future autonomous malware, where connectivity, latency, privacy, or operational constraints may preclude cloud-based inference. Paper:
title: Model Checking for Noisy Toric Words
summary: Toric words have recently gained attention as a means to model the behaviour of dynamical systems such as linear loops. This work is concerned with describing when the toric model is precise enough to decide whether the trace of a system is contained in an omega-regular language. Our contributions are threefold. (i) We use topological means to generalise a class of toric words by defining noise-robust dynamical systems and their sets of noisy traces. We prove that all noisy traces of a system are almost-periodic, and have the same set of recurrent factors. (ii) We apply the abstract techniques above to concrete sequences obtained as sign descriptions of real algebraic linear recurrence sequences (LRS), and show that the language-membership problem for sign descriptions of LRS with few dominant roots is decidable. (iii) We show that noisy traces of noise-robust dynamical systems are indistinguishable to a prefix-independent omega-regular language, and inclusion is decidable provided the common language of their recurrent factors is recursive. We incidentally obtain properties of prefix-independent omega-regular languages that may be of independent interest.

title: Actions with Receipts: Jointly Binding Claims, Evidence, and Execution for Replayable Tool-Agent Auditing
summary: Tool-using agents can expose citations and execution logs while leaving a critical association unaudited: whether the claim shown to a user is the claim emitted by the committed execution and supported by the cited source. We separate this integrity plane from a pluggable support plane, so structural validity is not used as a proxy for entailment. Paper:
title: Monitor-Validity Failures: LLM Safety Evidence Paths at Evolving Framework Boundaries
summary: Modern LLM applications rely on runtime monitors that inspect tool calls, traces, streams, detector outputs, and verifier inputs. This creates an interface-reliability problem: a framework path may remain operational while policy-relevant evidence never reaches its decision point. In one representative case, a regex detector returned a positive match, but the framework stranded the result before the block decision. This differs from jailbreaks and detector errors because the evidence is already recognized yet disconnected from enforcement. We study this repair-boundary signature with canary contracts: parent/fixed confirmation units that place a known payload only on the changed evidence surface and record monitor visibility together with the downstream decision for action-boundary cases. Applying the protocol to public framework repairs, we confirm 18 evidence-path failures across 11 LLM or agent safety project groups and four implementation ecosystems. Nine are established-boundary repairs, eight are new-surface policy-coverage gaps, and one is a boundary-only evidence case. Fourteen reach E1 enforcement boundaries: seven native action outcomes, six configured enforcement boundaries, and one synthetic-consumer consequence. The remaining cases affect verifier, safety-prompt, or observability channels. The cases form carrier, adapter, authority, and surface families and show how ordinary application behavior can remain intact while a safety-specific evidence path misses its decision. Exact revisions, deterministic outcomes, negative controls, and a frozen prospective audit document the confirmation rule. Monitor assumptions therefore need regression tests at the schemas, streams, tools, and adapters that frameworks evolve.

Paper:
title: Merge Hulls Without Copying Vertices: GPU Isotonic Regression
summary: Isotonic regression finds the monotone sequence closest to the data in weighted least squares. It is used to calibrate probabilities and inside differentiable ranking. Its standard algorithm, pool adjacent violators, is sequential within a sequence, and torchsort, the exact GPU solver of differentiable sorting libraries, runs it with one thread per sequence, which is slow on long ones. The fit is the slope sequence of the lower convex hull of cumulative sums, and hulls of sorted points can be merged in parallel. Merging partial hulls level by level, however, copies the surviving vertices at every level, which moves $Θ(n \log n)$ data when most points survive. We store each chunk's hull once and represent a merged hull as a list of segments of these chunk hulls, at most one per chunk; a merge then updates the list. We prove the representation correct, bound the work and depth of the merge phase, and measure a CUDA implementation on four NVIDIA GPUs against a control that copies the surviving vertices with the whole GPU at every level. On dense hulls the merge phase is 17 to 276 times faster with segment lists and the whole operator 3.9 to 19 times; on noisy data, where few vertices survive, the difference is small. In a differentiable soft rank, replacing torchsort's isotonic solver makes forward and backward 2.3 to 230 times faster on a T4, and the training step of a compact model with a Spearman loss 1.6 to 9 times.

title: VStress: Correlation-Aware Auditing and Adaptive Budget Allocation for Repeated Verifiers
summary: Repeated verifier calls are useful only when they contribute conditional information. Paper:
title: Practical and Private Hybrid ML Inference with Fully Homomorphic Encryption
summary: In contemporary cloud-based services, protecting users' sensitive data and ensuring the confidentiality of the server's model are critical. Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables inference directly on encrypted inputs, but its practicality is hindered by expensive bootstrapping and inefficient approximations of non-linear activations. We introduce Safhire, a hybrid inference framework that executes linear layers under encryption on the server while offloading non- linearities to the client in plaintext. This design eliminates bootstrapping, supports exact activations, and significantly reduces computation cost. To safeguard model confidentiality despite client access to intermediate outputs, Safhire applies randomized shuffling, which obfuscates intermediate values and makes it practically impossible for a client to reconstruct the model. To further reduce inference latency, Safhire incorporates advanced optimizations such as fast ciphertext packing and partial extraction. Evaluations on multiple standard models and datasets show that Safhire achieves up to 7.6x and 7.4x lower inference latency than Orion and Concrete-ML, respectively, which are two state-of-the-art FHE baselines, with manageable communication overhead and comparable accuracy. These results underline the practicality of our hybrid FHE inference scheme.

Paper:
title: CascadeLedger: Counterfactual Auditing of Information and Resource Integrity in LLM Cascades
summary: We introduce CascadeLedger, a counterfactual execution-audit framework for budgeted language-model cascades. The protocol enforces call-before-read semantics, binds successful reads to service and cache identities, records availability and component-wise budget transitions, and freezes the event trace before any target or task scorer is joined. The central object is aggregate-equivalent trace validity: two executions can share a final answer, declared resource projection, and service histogram while differing in whether their routing decisions used only legitimately observable information. We complement single-trace invariants with counterfactual prefix non-interference (CPNI), which couples a visible prefix and policy randomness while changing only a declared hidden family. The counterfactual influence frontier (CIF) localizes the earliest violating prefix and a minimal hidden witness; projection-preserving adversarial mutation (PPAM) searches for invalid traces that remain acceptable to a non-counterfactual checker. Across frozen-cache, independently generated, and serving evaluations, the two-layer audit reports a clean false-positive rate of 0.0000, detects 0.9983 of serialized faults and 0.9982 of unlogged hidden-read faults, and changes 0.3403 of corrupted quality-resource conclusions after deterministic recomputation. The online recorder and offline CPNI audit have separate overhead measurements. Learned routing and semantic verification provide downstream compatibility studies under the same execution contract.

title: MobileInject: Evaluating Reasoning-to-Action Security of MLLM-Based Mobile Agents under Cross-Modal Consistency Injection
summary: Multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based mobile agents are rapidly evolving from conversational assistants into autonomous systems that perceive, reason over, and act on smartphone environments. This capability also exposes a new security risk: adversaries can embed malicious objectives in cross-application mobile content and steer agent behavior through indirect multimodal injection. Systematic experiments show that mobile agents are broadly vulnerable to multimodal injection, and that many failures stem from reasoning hijacking at early stages. These findings establish MobileInject as a systematic cross-modal benchmark for studying and improving the security of mobile agents. Paper:
title: On the (In)stability of Adaptive Fee Mechanisms in Multi-Chain Systems
summary: EIP-1559 has become the dominant transaction fee mechanism in permissionless blockchains, regulating scarce block space through an adaptive base fee. The design balances a trade-off between responsiveness to demand fluctuations and stability of long-term resource usage. On a single chain, this trade-off is well understood and empirically stable. In multi-chain systems, however, cross-chain flows introduce delayed economic interactions across otherwise independent fee markets. These interactions alter the control dynamics and create stability risks that existing models do not capture. Deployed systems have already polarized. Polkadot enforces conservative update rates, effectively disabling fee adaptivity and reverting the market to inefficient first-price auctions. Cosmos adopts aggressive update rates without formal guarantees.
  To fill this gap, we propose a control-theoretic framework that formalizes multi-chain fee markets as a nonlinear dynamical system with delayed feedback. We identify delay-amplified over-correction as the structural root of instability. Experiments show that cross-chain coupling erodes stability relative to monolithic blockchains, reducing the safe parameter space for base fee update rates by up to 84.8%. Moreover, instability propagates across chains, contaminating the otherwise stable peer chains. At Ethereum's update rate, which leaves a monolithic chain stable, the multi-chain system exhibits extreme load oscillation between full and near-empty blocks, with over half of all blocks at full capacity. Mainstream Cosmos chains already exceed their safe bounds under their default configurations, and the resulting load oscillation raises their block failure rate by an order of magnitude. Guided by this mechanism, we design a lightweight protocol-level mitigation that removes the over-correction and stabilizes dynamics in multi-chain environments.

Paper:
title: MobileJailBench: Red Queen Jailbreak Benchmarking for Mobile Agents
summary: MLLM-based mobile agents are rapidly gaining autonomy in perception, planning, and closed-loop execution in dynamic mobile environments. However, this autonomy also broadens the attack surface and amplifies the risks of malicious misuse, including privacy leakage, device compromise, and large-scale phishing. Existing jailbreak evaluations leave three critical gaps for mobile agents: they focus on conversational attacks instead of mobile workflows, use static task sets with fixed difficulty, and rely narrowly on attack success rate rather than comprehensive security assessment. To close these gaps, we present MobileJailBench, the first evolving jailbreak benchmark for mobile agents, comprising three key components: (1) a benchmark comprising 520 tasks spanning three jailbreak paradigms and 14 risk categories, built on a high-fidelity mobile sandbox that we construct, enabling realistic workflows across over 20 widely used apps; (2) Dual-Dynamic Evolution, which combines Failure-Distilled Jailbreak Evolution with Weakness-Driven Benchmark Expansion; and (3) Stratified Adjudication Framework for assessing security awareness, execution behavior, and risk consequences. Extensive experiments show that current mobile agents are particularly vulnerable to implicit jailbreaks, as their safety alignment remains largely superficial and fails to generalize from conversational refusal to dynamic mobile interactions. Moreover, our dynamic evolution mechanism sharpens practical threat boundaries by continually uncovering new vulnerabilities, reaching a 100% ASR on Qwen3.5-122B. MobileJailBench provides a reproducible, continuously evolving framework for tracking the true security boundaries of mobile agents.

Paper:
title: Ignored, Not Refused: What Low Prompt-Injection Success Rates Hide in Small Tool-Using Agents
summary: Tool-using agents read untrusted external content, which exposes them to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where hidden instructions hijack the agent's tool calls. Benchmarks measure IPI security by the attack success rate (ASR), which treats every failed attack as a successful defense. To test this assumption, we audit 33,000 trajectories from eleven open-weight agents (2-14B parameters) on InjecAgent and AgentDojo. A label-blind LLM judge shows that most failed attacks are ignored (76-80%) rather than refused (17-18%). With identical model weights, changing only the system prompt shifts InjecAgent ASR from 0.2% to 43%. Our Attack-Task Outcome Matrix (ATOM) further shows that in 21.7% of AgentDojo episodes, the agent stayed safe but did not complete the user's task. A low ASR therefore mostly reflects agents silently ignoring injections, not refusing them. Evaluations should report how attacks fail and whether the user's task is completed, alongside ASR. We release the labeled corpus, judge prompt, and analysis code.

Paper:
title: Evidence-Bound Gateway-Path Provenance for Third-Party LLM Inference
summary: Third-party LLM gateways select providers, models, endpoints, and fallback paths while also authoring the records used to explain and bill those decisions. We present evidence-bound gateway-path provenance, which makes these decisions subject to client-verifiable request contracts. An attested mediation runtime intersects a signed service policy with the client's authorization, constructs provider-facing calls, and protects streamed responses. The contract distinguishes initial routes from fallback destinations and admits each transition only after an authorized failure. A signed close-out binds the execution trace, provider-reported usage, authorized pricing, and complete response. We formalize the protocol state machine and establish authorization preservation, execution and stream binding, charge integrity, and channel confidentiality relative to the public receipt metadata. The analysis also characterizes replay, runtime replacement, and the information disclosed by public payload commitments. Controlled software-path measurements show 0.442 ms paired p95 latency overhead at concurrency one, peak throughput of 10.65 thousand requests/s, and stream close-out below 0.4 ms p95. An AWS Nitro Enclaves prototype completed 30 live single-route streaming requests with attestation-bound session and signing keys. The design separates gateway administration from payload processing and supplies a verifiable account of each confirmed execution.

Paper:
title: A Deeper Dive into the Irreversibility of PolyProtect: Making Protected Face Templates Harder to Invert
summary: This work presents a deeper analysis of the "irreversibility" property of PolyProtect, a biometric template protection method initially proposed for securing face embeddings. PolyProtect transforms embeddings into protected templates via multivariate polynomials, whose coefficients and exponents are distinct for each subject enrolled in the face recognition system. A polynomial is applied to consecutive sets of elements from a given embedding, where the amount of overlap between the sets is a tunable parameter. We begin our irreversibility analysis by demonstrating that PolyProtected templates are easier to invert using a numerical solver based on cosine distance, as opposed to Euclidean distance (used in the earlier PolyProtect work). To make this inversion more difficult, we then propose a "key selection algorithm", which tries to choose "keys" (coefficients and exponents of the PolyProtect polynomial) that enhance the irreversibility of PolyProtected templates, compared to when the keys are purely random. Our experiments show that this algorithm is effective at generating PolyProtected templates that are significantly more difficult to invert, and that it approximately equalises the irreversibility of PolyProtected templates generated using different "overlap" parameters. This allows for better control of the known irreversibility versus accuracy trade-off across different overlaps. We also show that accuracy in the PolyProtected domain can be affected by the range in which the embedding elements lie, but that this can be improved by normalizing the embeddings prior to applying PolyProtect. This work is reproducible using our open-source code: https://github.com/idiap/BTPBench/blob/main/paper/polyprotect-irreversibility/.

Paper:
title: An AI Approach to Verified Production Cryptographic Libraries
summary: Cryptographic code is critical infrastructure that must be correct, yet formally verifying production libraries remains difficult. Existing language-model proof systems solve isolated obligations with specifications and premises already given, leaving production-library verification unresolved.
  We present CryptoProver, an AI-based system that synthesizes internal specifications and Verus-checked proofs from high-level API contracts. Without changing executable code, CryptoProver constructs a new independent proof of curve25519-dalek and verifies RustCrypto's previously unverified chacha20 implementation against an RFC 8439 specification. These cryptographic lineages underpin deployed systems including Signal and Shadowsocks; Signal has an estimated 218M global downloads. The original developers report a focused five-month, three-person effort to verify curve25519-dalek. Given the API contracts and a fixed trusted library of field specifications, arithmetic facts, axioms, and vstd, CryptoProver synthesizes the internal specifications and proofs in 11.4 hours with USD 466.99 in recorded API cost. CryptoProver follows a trust-first design principle: mechanical gates reject specification weakening, invented axioms, and cross-module breakage, while isolation blocks reference proof retrieval, including from git history.

Paper:
title: Trojan Horse: Automated Repository Poisoning against Coding Agents
summary: Coding agents are increasingly capable with autonomy, which exposes them to repository-level poisoning. Existing red-teaming studies remain restricted to manual selection for malicious payload locations and fixed disguise strategies, which cannot represent realistic repository poisoning. We present TrojanForge, the first automated framework for repository poisoning. TrojanForge parses repository structure through abstract syntax trees (AST) and maps agent execution traces onto AST nodes. A security review agent ranks these candidates and selects the least conspicuous ones for payload mounting. Then, through adversarial play with the target agent, TrojanForge iteratively refines disguise strategies by inverting the causes of agent detection, and transfers accumulated success experience across repositories. We further construct TrojanBench, a benchmark of 384 poisoned repositories spanning 6 domains and 9 programming languages. Extensive experiments show that TrojanForge achieves a stable poisoning success rate of over 60% with backdoor injection exceeding 90%. Comprehensive evaluation on TrojanBench across 4 harnesses and 12 models reveals that even commercial agents fail to defend against repository-level poisoning.

Paper:
title: Distributed Stochastic Momentum Tracking with Local Updates: Achieving Optimal Communication Complexities
summary: We propose Local Momentum Tracking (LMT), a novel distributed stochastic gradient method for solving distributed optimization problems over networks. To reduce communication overhead, LMT enables each agent to perform multiple local updates between consecutive communication rounds. Specifically, LMT integrates local updates with the momentum tracking strategy and the Loopless Chebyshev Acceleration (LCA) technique. We demonstrate that LMT achieves linear speedup with respect to the number of local updates as well as the number of agents for minimizing smooth objective functions with and without the Polyak-Łojasiewicz (PL) condition. In particular, LMT outperforms existing distributed stochastic gradient methods with local updates, and notably attains the optimal communication complexities with sufficiently many local updates $Q\geq Q^*$. For a moderate number of local updates $Q=\mathcal{O}(1)$, the performance of LMT matches the best known result for $Q=1$ under smooth nonconvex objectives, and improves upon it under the PL condition. For $Q=1$, we further establish minimax performance lower bounds over two comparison families. For smooth objectives, LMT matches the lower bound. For PL objectives, LMT attains the minimax-optimal dependence on the spectral gap, up to logarithmic factors. To our knowledge, LMT is the first distributed stochastic gradient method with local updates that enjoys such properties.

Paper:
title: Concrete Functions in Private Simultaneous Quantum Messages: Quantum Advantages and Structural Limitations
summary: Private simultaneous quantum messages (PSQM) provide a minimal model of noninteractive secure multiparty quantum computation, yet their communication complexity for concrete functions remains poorly understood. We show that familiar total functions already exhibit both genuine quantum advantages and strong structural limitations. For three-party equality on $n$-bit inputs, which determines whether the players' $n$-bit strings are identical, we construct an entanglement-assisted protocol with asymptotic communication $(1.633\ldots)n$ qubits, whereas every perfectly correct protocol without prior entanglement requires at least $3n$ qubits. For three-bit majority, one shared GHZ state and one transmitted qubit per player suffice for perfect correctness and perfect privacy, reducing the communication from the optimal classical cost of six bits to three qubits. Three-bit AND behaves differently. No perfectly correct and perfectly private protocol exists when the players share an arbitrary three-qubit state, apply arbitrary local unitary encodings, and transmit one qubit each. However, increasing the local dimension overcomes this obstruction: one shared three-qutrit GHZ state and one transmitted qutrit per player yield a one-shot protocol with total communication $3\log_2 3$. Together with the six-bit classical lower bound, this gives a strict quantum communication advantage. More generally, for every $k\geq 3$, we construct a perfectly correct and perfectly private one-shot protocol for $k$-bit AND using one qudit of dimension at most $k$ per player, and hence at most $k\log_2 k$ qubits in total.

Paper:
title: Cryptographically Secure Agent-to-Agent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) comprise AI agents that collaborate or compete to perform complex, distributed tasks. Their dynamic interactions create opportunities for threat actors to target and impersonate other agents, intercept messages, inject malicious prompts, and exfiltrate sensitive data while simultaneously complicating the detection of anomalous behavior through conventional monitoring. This paper surveys threats and cryptographic challenges in agent-to-agent communication and presents a zero-trust architecture integrating identity, transport security, message integrity, and monitoring. The architecture establishes agent identities via decentralized identifiers and task-scoped verifiable credentials backed by a permissioned ledger, enforcing least-privilege authorization. For transport security, it provides mutually authenticated, crypto-agile TLS with hybrid post-quantum key establishment, and evaluates KEMTLS with pre-distributed public keys to reduce handshake overhead. Signed CBOR envelopes preserve payload integrity across multi-hop exchanges, while zero-knowledge proofs verify declared task constraints without exposing underlying inputs. Context-aware monitoring of inter-agent messages, tool activity, and execution telemetry informs the setting of risk-based trust thresholds and supports the detection of behavioral anomalies. Together, these mechanisms provide an integrated framework for securing and auditing agent communication, with implications for other agentic protocols and prospective 6G semantic communication.

Paper:
title: When Approval Becomes Execution: Authorization-Grounded Workflow Attacks on Tool-Using Agents
summary: Tool-using language-model agents increasingly rely on local services for document access, approval management, and enterprise workflow execution. This paper studies an authorization-grounded workflow attack in the OpenClaw Agent Security Attack Competition, a controlled benchmark derived from SeClaw-style security task synthesis. Rather than using explicit policy-override instructions, the attack guides the agent through a locally coherent approval workflow: a protected document request is denied, the agent requests a normal approval token from the local approval service, and the returned token is supplied to the document service through authorized_by. Official submission traces show this pattern succeeding on three Enterprise OA document targets. We also conducted 23 controlled local validation experiments in the official OpenClaw execution environment: the original configuration reached the approval-token transition in 9/9 reruns and completed the exact target operation in 8/9 reruns, while single-component variants remained successful on the three document targets. The results provide concrete case evidence of an authorization-context gap: token possession can be treated as sufficient authorization even when requester identity, approver authority, resource scope, action type, destination or recipient, and business purpose are not jointly enforced. We present the attack pattern, controlled trace analysis, and defensive implications for context-bound tokens, service-side policy binding, agent-side authorization checks, and trace-aware benchmark design.

Paper:
title: ScaleRAN: A Runtime for Elastic GPU Resource Management in AI-RAN
summary: AI-RAN is driving the convergence of radio access network (RAN) processing and artificial intelligence (AI) workloads on GPU-enabled computing platforms, ranging from GPU-accelerated base stations to cloud-native infrastructures. While GPU acceleration improves the efficiency of virtualized RAN functions, the computational demand of latency-critical baseband processing varies with traffic load, creating transient spare GPU capacity that can be reclaimed by co-located AI applications. Existing GPU-sharing mechanisms rely on coarse-grained hardware partitioning or static resource allocation, limiting their ability to adapt to slot-level workload fluctuations while preserving strict timing requirements.
  This paper presents ScaleRAN, a node-local runtime for elastic GPU resource management in AI-RAN. ScaleRAN leverages NVIDIA Green Contexts to dynamically partition Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) between RAN and AI workloads through a ladder of pre-created GPU partitions, enabling low-overhead resource reallocation at RAN slot granularity. The proposed runtime naturally supports Open-RAN (O-RAN) O-Cloud deployments, one representative AI-RAN deployment scenario. To drive these reallocations, we propose a reactive controller inspired by Kubernetes autoscaling and a proactive controller based on quantile regression and conformal prediction. We also develop LDPCSim, a GPU-accelerated workload generator built on NVIDIA Aerial for reproducible evaluation. Results show that predictive fine-grained GPU partitioning satisfies slot-level RAN deadlines while increasing the GPU resources available to co-located AI workloads, demonstrating the practicality of elastic GPU sharing for future AI-RAN platforms.

Paper:
title: BaGuaLu-2: Taming Dynamic Memory Fluctuation for Efficient MoE Model Training over 10,000 GPUs
summary: Fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is the de facto architecture for scaling large language models. However, dynamic expert load imbalance causes severe memory fluctuations that degrade training efficiency. Existing systems rely on static memory provisioning: they either over-provision, leaving GPU memory idle during normal execution, or under- provision, inviting out-of-memory crashes and costly manual rollbacks when load spikes occur. To address these challenges, we propose BaGuaLu-2, a large-scale MoE training system that eliminates this dilemma through flexible provisioning. By transforming memory allocation from a static, one-time tuning choice into a continuous and fine-grained control. BaGuaLu-2 grants exact activation memory on demand for each training batch. Furthermore, it offsets any dynamic management overhead through system optimizations. BaGuaLu-2 demonstrates exceptional scalability, training a model with 1040 billion parameters across 12,288 GPUs while sustaining over 2 EFlops at 35% MFU. Compared with state-of-the-art systems, BaGuaLu-2 delivers 1.14x and 1.13x average throughput improvements over Megatron-Kuai and AdaPipe, respectively.

Paper:
title: Aspire: Practical Batch Queries on Dynamic Encrypted Database with Full Leakage Suppression
summary: Leakage-abuse attacks against encrypted database systems exploit semantic leakage and pose a severe threat to the confidentiality of plaintext data and queries. To address this problem, we propose a zero-leakage encrypted database that rules out leakage-abuse attacks, which fundamentally rely on semantic leakage. We first distinguish between two kinds of zero-leakage security. Ideal zero-leakage forbids the disclosure of any information beyond public parameters, whereas restricted zero-leakage additionally permits the leakage of metadata (such as database size and query timing). We show that restricted zero-leakage is sufficient to thwart leakage-abuse attacks and is achievable in practice. We then formally define adaptive restricted zero-leakage security and present Aspire, an encrypted database that satisfies this notion. Aspire integrates probabilistic batch code and minimal perfect hashing to support efficient batch keyword queries and dynamic updates while revealing only non-semantic metadata. Experimental results demonstrate the practicality and efficiency of Aspire, showing that Aspire can achieve an amortized query latency of less than 1.38 ms (7.53 s for a batch of 5461 keyword queries), with an amortized communication cost of approximately 2.95 KB (16.1 MB in total), on a $2^{22}$ key-value pairs database.
